newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dollar surge heralds windfall for German exporters.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surge heralds windfall for German exporters.

text.p: Export-driven Germany can afford to breathe a sigh of relief as the dollar's surge against the mark promises windfall profits for struggling exporters, analysts said this week.
"For a country which is about the most export-driven of the major economies, this is the best we could have hoped for," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch, Germany.
The dollar was on Wednesday trading around 1.64 marks, its highest level since June 1994 and some 13 percent up on last year's low of 1.45 marks.

This, economists and analysts agree, should mean a real boost for Germany's car-makers, engineering firms and chemical firms, who stand to regain competitive edge on pricing and make significantly more in mark terms on their foreign earnings.
"Exports were already well up in the latter part of 1996 and this dollar move means the strong growth can continue," Schmieding said.

The message is feeding through to the stock market, where exporters' shares were strongly ahead on the blue chip DAX index Wednesday, which is currently hitting record levels of well above 3,000 points.

Daimler-Benz AG, arguably the DAX's most dollar-sensitive firm after blaming a large chunk of its record 5.7 billion mark ($3.5 billion) loss in 1995 on the strong mark, has risen almost twice as fast as the DAX this year, with gains of nine percent.

"The stronger dollar will benefit all of Germany's export oriented companies," said a Daimler spokeswoman, adding that Daimler's chief goal remained to reduce its exposure to currency fluctuations by shifting production abroad.
"Hedging against mark appreciation is only a short term step," the spokeswoman noted.

Trinkaus Capital Management auto analyst Christian Breitsprecher, who upped his earnings per share forecasts for Daimler through to 1998 after the dollar broke over 1.60 marks said Daimler's strategy was sensible.
"The more Daimler actually produces abroad and the more it buys in, especially from the dollar area, the better its chances are," Breitsprecher said.

Germany's other biggest carmakers may benefit less from the dollar's surge. BMW AG, for example, has recently opened a U.S. plant in South Carolina in an effort to cut its dollar exposure while VW already has two major units outside Germany and plans to produce its new Beetle model in Mexico.
But analysts warned that, unless companies act now to hedge their positions against further fluctuations, a move some cannot afford, more trouble could be ahead.
"German engineering firms are certainly going to get windfall profits, there's no doubt about it," said Juergen Warfsmann, engineering analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG in Munich.

"But the overall profit situation in the engineering sector is pretty strained," Warfsmann added. "Margins were about one to 1.5 percent in 1996. But if the dollar holds at this level, we could see 1.5 percent to 2.5 percent this year."
And the outlook for German consumer demand this year remains muted.

Merrill Lynch's Schmieding said he was still expecting moderate German growth of some 2.5 percent this year although he recently increased his forecast for export growth to seven percent from 5.5 percent while slightly scaling back his expectations for growth in consumer demand.
Latest available German output data showed exports by far outstripping domestic business, with exports rising 14 percent in November against an overall output advance of 1.6 percent.
The greatest risk to German profits is presented by the dollar itself.
"It's a very risky business trying to predict where a currency will go, commented Trinkaus' Breitsprecher.
"We could be right back down at 1.45 (marks to the dollar) before we know it," he added.
